source.title: Measuring Mechanistic Independence: Can Bias Be Removed Without Erasing Demographics?

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Applies pretrained SAE feature identification and ablation to Gemma models, and reports outcomes bearing on whether SAE features can serve as useful recovered features in an LLM. It does not test superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: Included reported SAE-feature ablation outcomes as indirect evidence about recovered features in an LLM. The paper's baseline demographic accuracies, feature-selection rankings, and cited results are not rows: they do not independently test the claim versions. The full ablation tables contain additional task/method combinations beyond the representative results recorded here.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained Gemma-Scope SAE features as a tool to locate and ablate demographic-bias features in Gemma-2-9B-IT. It reports only its debiasing method's effects on bias (KL) and name accuracy. It does not measure superposition, polysemanticity, feature spread across neurons, SAE recovery quality, completeness or canonicity, or feature dimensionality. An ablation that changes bias is evidence about the intervention, not about whether SAEs recover the model's features, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is mostly right. It should add the authors' headline claim. They say targeted SAE ablations in Gemma-2-9B reduce race and gender bias while preserving name recognition. They also say stereotypical and recognition mechanisms are largely independent, and that bias arises from task-specific mechanisms. Correlation ablation works better for education bias, where attribution ablation causes 'prior collapse'.
record.recipe_differences: Uses pretrained Gemma-Scope SAE features, attribution/correlation selection, and activation ablation in demographic tasks; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition setup or measure its geometric transitions.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by demographic dimension, feature-selection method, source task, and prompt format (Demo-R versus Demo-L).
record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (venue stated in supplied metadata)
record.problems: Evidence is limited to English-language tasks and the Gemma-2 family for mechanistic interventions. The authors note that SAE dictionaries do not exhaustively cover model internals and that ablations can have side effects. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported ablation outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix C, Tables C.6-C.7 report additional ablation-method and cross-task metric combinations; they are omitted here because the recorded rows give the principal stated outcomes bearing on SAE-derived feature effects, rather than an exhaustive catalog of demographic-bias outcomes. Appendix E, Table E.9 reports additional Winogender metrics, which are not direct measurements of SAE feature recovery or superposition geometry.

untested.parts: All of V1: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All of V2: no capacity competition or neuron polysemanticity analysis.
All of V3: no analysis of the causes of polysemantic neurons.
All of V4: SAEs are used, but there is no measure of feature spread across neurons or of SAE recovery or reconstruction quality.
All of V5: SAE completeness, stability and canonicity are not tested. The authors only remark in their limitations that SAEs are not exhaustive.
All of V6: no comparison of 1-D and multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: This is a debiasing application paper that uses Gemma-Scope SAEs as an off-the-shelf tool. The reader's V4 'supports' label is unfounded: changing a bias metric by ablating SAE latents does not show the model stores sparse features that the SAE recovers. Appendix G.2 notes that available Llama SAEs gave zero or too-low attribution scores. That concerns tool usability, not superposition.

versions.untested_parts: No test of toy networks, feature sparsity or co-activation, overlap, near-orthogonal geometry, or a sparsity-dependent transition.
No test of capacity competition, dedicated versus shared dimensions, or neuron polysemanticity.
No test of polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Tests SAE-derived features in Gemma models, but does not measure feature distribution across neurons, feature sparsity, or whether SAE recovery captures features generally or completely.

Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable across settings, or canonical units; the authors' limitation that SAEs do not exhaustively cover model internals is not an experimental test of those properties.
No comparison of one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Ablating SAE-derived features changes recognition and profession/education prediction outcomes, showing task-relevant effects for recovered features in this tested setting (r1-r10). The results do not establish feature geometry or broad recovery coverage.
